headline: ESBMC-ARDUINO: CLOSING THE DEPLOYMENT GAP FOR FORMAL VERIFICATION OF OPEN-HARDWARE PLCS
name: ESBMC-ARDUINO: CLOSING THE DEPLOYMENT GAP FOR FORMAL VERIFICATION OF OPEN-HARDWARE PLCS
description: scan-cycle model with idealized unbounded integers. The artifact that runs on the board, however, executes on a resource-constrained Microcontroller Unit (MCU) with a 16-bit machine word (8-bit AVR Arduinos), and sensors are read through a finite-resolution Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). We show that this deployment gap makes naive width-aware verification unsound in practice: on 123 real third-party programs, checking 16-bit arithmetic overflow without a hardware input model raises a 44 % false-alarm rate (54/123) and finds zero genuine defects, because it explores sensor values no ADC can produce. Because the gap sits exactly where computation meets the physical process – a bounded sensor reading scaled by finite-width integer arithmetic into an actuation command – an overflow can silently suppress a physical safety action such as a high-level alarm. At the same time, an unbounded input model fabricates alarms that no environment can trigger. We present a method for hardware-faithful verification of IEC 61131-3 on open hardware: a declarative Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) descriptor (word width, ADC/Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) resolution, I/O binding) and a sound lowering that interprets arithmetic at the target word width and constrains each input to its hardware-realizable range, transferring to the Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) domain the target-model discipline established for safety-critical embedded C (Frama-C, Astrée). We instantiate it for Arduino as ESBMC-Arduino, deriving HAL parameters from the official Arduino cores and realizing the input-range model as a lightweight hook in the Efficient SMT-based Context-Bounded Model Checker (ESBMC) Ladder Diagram (LD) frontend. On the 123-program corpus, the HAL annotator eliminates all 54 false alarms (54→0) while preserving every robustness proof, and a controlled corpus demonstrates the genuine – but rare – width-dependent defects the method detects with physically realizable witnesses.

hasPart.name: 1. Introduction
hasPart.description: Introduces the context of open-hardware PLCs and the problem of the deployment gap between abstract formal verification models and resource-constrained microcontroller execution.

hasPart.name: 1.1 The Deployment Gap
hasPart.description: Details the specific discrepancies arising from hardware limitations like finite bit-widths and ADC resolution that invalidate abstract verification assumptions.

hasPart.name: 1.2 Contributions
hasPart.description: Outlines the primary technical contributions of the work, including hardware-faithful verification and the ESBMC-Arduino framework.

hasPart.name: 1.3 Scope
hasPart.description: Defines the boundaries and specific hardware classes targeted within the scope of this study.

hasPart.name: 2. Background
hasPart.description: Provides necessary background on PLC scan cycles, open-hardware toolchains, PLCopen XML representation, and machine models of Arduino-class targets.

hasPart.name: 2.1 The PLC Scan Cycle
hasPart.description: Explains the standard cyclic execution model of Programmable Logic Controllers involving input reading, logic execution, and output writing.

hasPart.name: 2.2 Open-Hardware PLCs and the OpenPLC Toolchain
hasPart.description: Describes open-hardware PLC platforms and how the OpenPLC toolchain compiles IEC 61131-3 code into target microcontroller binaries.

hasPart.name: 2.4 PLCopen XML
hasPart.description: Discusses the XML-based standard format used to serialize PLC programs across different development environments.

hasPart.name: 2.5 From PLCopen XML to a Binary: the OpenPLC Toolchain
hasPart.description: Traces the compilation pipeline transforming high-level PLCopen XML specifications into executable microcontroller machine code.

hasPart.name: 2.6 Machine Models of Arduino-Class Targets
hasPart.description: Analyzes the architectural characteristics, memory constraints, and data type widths typical of Arduino-class microcontrollers.

hasPart.name: 2.7 Bounded Model Checking andk-Induction for PLCs
hasPart.description: Reviews the foundational formal verification techniques of bounded model checking and k-induction applied to industrial control systems.

hasPart.name: 3. Related Work
hasPart.description: Surveys existing literature concerning IEC 61131-3 verification, target-faithful analysis of embedded software, and code-generation correctness.

hasPart.name: 3.1 Verification of IEC 61131-3
hasPart.description: Examines prior approaches and tools designed to formally verify safety properties in IEC 61131-3 industrial programs.

hasPart.name: 3.2 Target-Faithful Analysis of Embedded Software
hasPart.description: Reviews methods that ensure software verification accounts for specific hardware target behaviors and constraints.

hasPart.name: 3.3 Code-Generation Correctness
hasPart.description: Discusses research on verifying the correctness of compilers and code generators targeting embedded systems.

hasPart.name: 4. The Deployment Gap, Formally
hasPart.description: Formalizes the concept of the deployment gap using physical process models, fault models, and motivating examples.

hasPart.name: 4.1 Physical Process and Fault Model
hasPart.description: Introduces the formal framework capturing physical plant interactions and potential hardware-induced software faults.

hasPart.name: 4.1.1 Fault model
hasPart.description: Defines the specific classes of faults considered, such as integer overflow and truncation errors caused by hardware limitations.

hasPart.name: 4.1.2 Assumptions
hasPart.description: Outlines the foundational assumptions regarding the environment, sensor resolution, and microcontroller behavior.

hasPart.name: 4.1.3 Motivating example
hasPart.description: Presents a concrete industrial control example where abstract verification fails to catch real hardware overflow behaviors.

hasPart.name: 5. Hardware-Faithful Verification
hasPart.description: Proposes the hardware-faithful verification framework, detailing scan-cycle execution models, faithful lowering, and soundness guarantees.

hasPart.name: 5.1 Scan-Cycle Execution Model
hasPart.description: Formulates an execution model that accurately reflects the discrete scan cycle of target hardware.

hasPart.name: 5.3 Faithful Lowering
hasPart.description: Describes the transformation process that preserves hardware semantics during intermediate representation generation.

hasPart.name: 5.4 Soundness and Gap Diagnosis
hasPart.description: Analyzes the soundness of the proposed verification approach and methods for diagnosing discrepancies caused by the deployment gap.

hasPart.name: 6.2 Implementation
hasPart.description: Details the software architecture and implementation details of the ESBMC-Arduino verification pipeline.

hasPart.name: 6.2.1 Where the Hook Sits
hasPart.description: Explains the integration point within the compilation and verification toolchain where hardware-specific checks are injected.

hasPart.name: 6.2.2 What the Hook Emits
hasPart.description: Details the assertions and code structures generated by the verification hook to capture hardware constraints.

hasPart.name: 6.2.3 Configurability and Engineering
hasPart.description: Discusses engineering choices and configuration options available to adapt the verifier to different microcontroller targets.

hasPart.name: 7. The Approach in Practice
hasPart.description: Demonstrates the practical application of the tool from both an engineer's perspective and an internal architectural viewpoint.

hasPart.name: 7.1.1 Engineer’s View
hasPart.description: Illustrates how control engineers interact with the ESBMC-Arduino tool during PLC application development.

hasPart.name: 7.1.2 Under the Hood
hasPart.description: Provides a deep dive into the internal mechanisms and solver interactions occurring during a verification run.

hasPart.name: 8. Evaluation
hasPart.description: Evaluates the performance, effectiveness, and soundness of ESBMC-Arduino across various benchmark programs and hardware targets.

hasPart.name: 8.1 Setup and Methodology
hasPart.description: Outlines the experimental setup, benchmark suites, and evaluation methodology used in the empirical study.

hasPart.name: 8.2 RQ1: The Gap Is Real but Rare
hasPart.description: Investigates research question 1, showing that deployment gaps occur in practice though they are relatively infrequent across standard benchmarks.

hasPart.name: 8.3 RQ2: Naive Width-Aware Verification Is Unusable
hasPart.description: Evaluates research question 2, demonstrating that naive application of bit-precise verification without proper modeling leads to severe scalability and usability issues.

hasPart.name: 8.4 RQ3: The HAL Annotator Restores Soundness
hasPart.description: Addresses research question 3, proving that hardware abstraction layer annotations successfully recover verification soundness.

hasPart.name: 8.5 Cross-Tool Validation: the Gap Is Not Tool-Specific
hasPart.description: Performs cross-tool validation to establish that the identified deployment gaps are inherent to the hardware-software interface rather than artifacts of a single verifier.

hasPart.name: 8.6 RQ4: Performance and Completeness
hasPart.description: Analyzes research question 4 regarding verification runtime overhead, scalability, and completeness of the proposed approach.

hasPart.name: 10. Threats to Validity
hasPart.description: Identifies potential internal and external validity threats to the experimental results and discusses mitigation strategies.

hasPart.name: 9. Discussion
hasPart.description: Synthesizes the broader implications of the findings for industrial control system security and formal verification tool design.

hasPart.name: 11. Future Work
hasPart.description: Outlines promising directions for future research, including support for more complex microcontroller architectures and richer hardware models.

hasPart.name: 12. Conclusion
hasPart.description: Summarizes the paper's core contributions in closing the deployment gap for open-hardware PLC verification using ESBMC-Arduino.
